sources.news_title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed due to weather for first time in 100 years - Regional Media News
sources.text:
By Kanishka Singh and Jasper Ward
Nov 25 (Reuters) – The 100th edition of the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City will be postponed for two days until Saturday due to forecasts of a major storm with high winds, marking the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.
“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s department store chain, which sponsors the event, said in a statement on Wednesday.
The three-hour parade through Manhattan, from 77th Street and Central Park West to Macy’s flagship store at Herald Square, is now set to commence at 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT) Saturday, the retailer said.
At an outdoor Thanksgiving-eve news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the choice to reschedule was coordinated with Macy’s, the New York Police Department and other agencies.
“We know that our city is the greatest city in the world, and we also know that in our city nothing comes easily, and you have to plan for every possibility,” he said.
Mamdani said gale-force winds forecast for Thursday, a situation that has previously interfered with the safety of the parade’s signature balloon displays, were a major factor in the decision to reschedule.
The parade was suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War Two, but has never been postponed before because of weather conditions.
The annual parade, televised nationwide, has become enmeshed in the traditions of America’s Thanksgiving holiday, a spectacle of huge inflatable cartoon characters, marching bands, clowns, cheerleaders and popular music acts performing live. Thousands line the streets of Manhattan to watch.
The National Weather Service has issued a high-wind warning and a coastal flood warning for New York City for Thursday into Friday.
The city was expected to face wind gusts of 50 to 60 miles per hour (80 to 96 kph) on Thursday, with sustained winds of 30 to 38 mph, the city’s emergency management office said.
Forecasters said this week that storms bringing heavy rain and winds up and down the US eastern seaboard were threatening to delay flights during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year.
Inclement weather has disrupted the parade before, including the 1997 procession when heavy wind gusts pushed a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, toppling a section of the street light into a crowd of onlookers below. Two people were hospitalized with head injuries.
Two other large balloons, inflatable likenesses of the Pink Panther and Barney the dinosaur, were also badly damaged in the blustery weather.
In response, then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani formed a task force to review the situation, leading to new size restrictions on the parade balloons and the removal of lampposts along the parade route.
All of the cartoon balloons that were brought into Manhattan and inflated in advance on Wednesday for this year’s event must now be deflated and returned to their facility in New Jersey and rendered “parade-ready” all over again, a process that normally takes a week, said Will Coss, head of Macy’s Studios.
City officials also are taking security factors into consideration, with an expanded NYPD presence planned along the parade route, despite an absence of any “known specific or credible threats” to the parade, city Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Jasper Ward in Washington and Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Writing and additional reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; editing by David Ljunggren, Nia Williams and Chris Reese)

NEW YORK, Nov 26 — New York has postponed the iconic Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday over fears of extreme weather, a first in the event’s 100-year history, as a major storm gathers steam on the US East Coast.
The brewing “nor’easter” threatens to disrupt plans for as many as 80 million people hitting the road and flying around the Thursday holiday, one of the country’s busiest travel seasons.
“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” parade sponsor Macy’s wrote in a statement shared by City Hall.
“Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, November 28.”
The annual parade sees brightly coloured balloons travel some 2.5 miles (four kilometres) from Midtown Manhattan to Macy’s Herald Square flagship store on 34th Street.
Millions of people typically gather to catch a glimpse of the festivities. It is the first time in its history that it has been postponed, The New York Post reported.
“This will be a heavy storm. We are expecting sustained winds between 30 and 40 miles per hour, with gusts as high as 60 to 65 miles per hour possible,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a safety briefing Wednesday.
“The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning as well as a coastal flood warning.
“Winds will be strong enough (Thursday) to down tree limbs and power lines.” Organizers would have been only too aware of the gusting winds that wrecked the parade in 1997.
Volunteers struggled but failed to keep a tight rein on ropes which constantly threatened to slam into onlookers.
The careening 18-foot figure of the “Cat in the Hat” – from the popular children’s book – toppled a lamppost, knocking one bystander unconscious.
Another balloon, the purple dinosaur known to children as “Barney,” went out of control prompting police armed with scissors to puncture and deflate the balloon.
Yet another casualty was the “Pink Panther” balloon, which blew up over 42nd Street, sending shreds of pink rubber confetti raining on bystanders.
“While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants – and spectators – is and always will be our top priority,” said Macy’s parade executive producer Will Coss. — AFP

sources.news_title: Bad weather postpones Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade for first time ever
sources.text:
Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: Organisers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday (November 28, 2026) because of bad weather.
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday (November 26, 2026), has been moved “out of an abundance of caution” and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy’s said in a statement Wednesday.
“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized,” the company said.
The postponement came as New York City is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade’s massive balloons would fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
At a news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday’s winds will be strong enough to snap tree limbs and down power lines, and he stressed that rescheduling the parade was the right call.
“Now, I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow,” he said. “Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first.”
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday. The city’s emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty tractor-trailers from bridges Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition on Thursday (November 26, 2026). It was not immediately clear whether the event’s expansive lineup would also shift to the new date, though representatives for Broadway shows “Chicago” and “Hamilton” said their performers will make the switch to Saturday (November 28, 2026).
The parade’s iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city’s news media ahead of the official postponement.
Will Coss, a Macy’s executive, said organizers are working with bands and other performers and are “optimistic that we’re going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce and to deliver to New York City on Thanksgiving.”
“Everyone understands what we’re up against and is rallying behind us to create the best and most successful 100th parade,” he said.
While the delay may have scrambled some parade-goers’ plans, the clouds had a silver lining for at least one youngster.
Sarah Collins and her youngest son have been looking forward to a New York weekend trip to celebrate his recent 12th birthday. But since their flight from Florida arrives Friday, the parade wasn’t part of their original plans. Now, it is, and he’s excited.
“It’s been his lifelong wish to go to New York and see all the Christmas stuff,” she said in a message.
A spokesperson for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was canceled for three years — in 1942, 1943 and 1944 — during World War II, the spokesperson said.
The parade balloons have been grounded only once due to weather, in 1971.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma. Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.

sources.text:
Storms push Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to Saturday
The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.
New York City is famous for its annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, a procession of towering helium balloons, elaborate floats and marching bands.
But on Wednesday, organisers in the United States announced that this year’s edition has been postponed because of an East Coast storm that threatens turbulent weather.
It was rescheduled for Saturday instead, right after Black Friday, a day when retailers traditionally offer holiday shopping and discount prices.
The annual parade is sponsored by Macy’s, a New York-based department store brand, and Saturday’s event will be its 100th Thanksgiving procession.
“While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority,” Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer, said in a Wednesday news conference.
“ We’re saddened by the shift, but we’re optimistic about our opportunity to deliver the most spectacular 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the best and biggest parade in our history.”
The parade, founded in 1924, was cancelled three times during World War II, but this year marks the first time it was postponed.
The event’s signature balloons were already being inflated on Wednesday when Macy’s announced the delay.
The decision came amid warnings issued by the National Weather Service of lashing winds and possible coastal flooding for the New York City area.
Gusts are forecast to reach up to 97 km/h, and rainfall of 2.5 to 5cm is expected from Thursday into Friday. A high wind warning is also in effect from 10am local time (15:00 GMT) Thursday through 1am (6:00 GMT) Friday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani described the decision as tough but necessary given the forecast.
“I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”
The holiday extravaganza typically draws more than 3.5 million spectators along its Manhattan route, according to New York City authorities. It is also broadcast nationwide.
For many Americans, the parade is a fixture of Thanksgiving, and the postponement marks a break with a familiar holiday ritual.
NBC, the television network that airs the annual parade, said it would instead broadcast a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday.
It remains unclear whether the full roster of performers scheduled for the parade will continue to perform on Saturday. According to Macy’s website, singers like Raye and Wyclef Jean were scheduled to headline, as were actors and Broadway stars like Leslie Odom Jr and Anthony Ramos.
New floats include a five-storey-tall balloon of the cartoon character Bluey wearing a crown, and a 17-meter-long version of the beagle Snoopy carrying his bird sidekick Woodstock.
There will also be a blue hippopotamus, a nod to the balloon that floated off from the 1931 parade and was lost.
Mamdani assured New Yorkers that the parade route would be safe once the storm passes on Saturday, thanks to a surge of law enforcement.
“ There will be an expanded police presence this Saturday along the route, and the [New York Police Department] is fully prepared for an event of this magnitude, just as they have been prepared for the 99 parades that preceded this,” Mamdani said.
“I want to make clear that there are no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time.”
The festivities are slated to begin at 8:30am local time (13:30 GMT).

sources.news_title: 100th Macy's Parade Moved to Saturday as Storm Nears
sources.text:
The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not march on Thanksgiving. New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's decided Wednesday afternoon to push the centennial parade to Saturday morning as a powerful coastal storm bore down on the Northeast, the first time in the event's history that weather has forced it off its holiday date.
The parade will now step off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 28, and NBC will carry the broadcast that morning instead of on Thursday. Officials from Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office confirmed the change shortly after Macy's announced it.
"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement. "We can't wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday."
The call came less than two hours after crews on Manhattan's Upper West Side had finished filling the parade's giant helium balloons, an annual eve-of-Thanksgiving ritual that draws thousands of spectators to the streets around the American Museum of Natural History. By Wednesday afternoon, some balloons were already lashed down with heavy ropes against the gusts. A city official said crews would begin deflating the balloons at 7 p.m. Wednesday and would inflate them again on Friday ahead of the rescheduled march.
The forecast left organizers little room. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for New York City covering Thursday into Friday. The outlook for Thanksgiving morning called for heavy rain, sustained winds of 20 to 22 mph and gusts near 40 mph around 9 a.m., with conditions expected to worsen through the day and some gusts forecast to approach 60 mph. Officials said gusts were forecast to reach or exceed the safety threshold used for balloon operations near the 8:30 a.m. start time.
That threshold is the product of hard experience. City rules adopted after a 1997 accident bar the giant balloons from flying if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph. That year, high winds drove the Cat in the Hat balloon into a light pole on the parade route, and the falling debris seriously injured a spectator. A second accident in 2005, when a balloon again struck a streetlight, led the city to tighten its balloon safety rules further.
Until this week, the standard response to bad weather had been to adjust the balloons rather than move the parade. Organizers have flown balloons at reduced heights in windy years, and weather has grounded them entirely only once before. Earlier in the week, city officials had floated similar options for Thursday, including starting the parade early to stay ahead of the worst conditions.
"This is a challenging week. This is a challenging forecast," New York City Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell said before the decision was made, adding that the city wanted the parade to be as safe as possible while keeping it iconic.
The postponement stands out against nearly a century of continuity. The parade began in 1924 as a Macy's employee procession featuring live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo, and the giant helium balloons arrived in 1927. It has been televised nationally on NBC since 1953. The only years it did not take place at all were 1942 through 1944, when it was suspended during World War II because the rubber and helium it relied on were needed for the war effort.
In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Macy's kept the Thanksgiving date but scrapped the traditional 2.5-mile route and the in-person crowds, staging a television-only event concentrated around its Herald Square flagship. Balloons that year were tethered to specially rigged vehicles instead of being guided by teams of handlers.
This year's postponement goes a step further. It moves the parade off Thanksgiving Day itself, the date that has defined the event for generations of families who watch from the sidewalks of Central Park West or from living rooms across the country. Macy's has said the parade typically draws about 3.5 million spectators along the route in a normal year and tens of millions of television viewers.
The 100th edition was built as a celebration of that legacy. Performers announced for this year's lineup include Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer and Natasha Bedingfield, alongside marching bands, Broadway casts and floats. Balloons inflated on Wednesday included longtime favorites Snoopy, Pikachu and Buzz Lightyear, and crews were also preparing the parade's signature Tom Turkey float.
Organizers have not said whether the full lineup of performers, bands and balloons will be able to take part on Saturday. Many marching bands and performers travel to New York from across the country for the event, and the two-day delay could test travel plans and hotel bookings for participants who had expected to head home after Thursday.
The route itself is expected to stay the same. The parade traditionally steps off near West 77th Street and Central Park West, heads south along the park and turns toward Midtown, ending outside Macy's Herald Square store on 34th Street.
The storm behind the decision is one of the largest to hit the East Coast during a Thanksgiving week in years. Forecasters expect it to deliver heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding from the mid-Atlantic to New England through Thanksgiving Day, with roughly 70 million people under wind alerts as the system strengthened Wednesday.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency that took effect at 6 p.m. Wednesday and is expected to last through Thursday, and officials in Atlantic City urged residents to evacuate ahead of a forecast surge of flooding along the Jersey Shore. Officials across the region have urged travelers to leave early or delay trips, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that the storm would be a challenge for holiday travel.
Conditions are expected to improve on Friday as the storm moves into New England and out to sea, giving organizers a clearer window for Saturday's march. Forecasters had already flagged Saturday as the best travel day of the holiday weekend for much of the country.
The move also scrambles holiday plans for the tens of thousands of New Yorkers and visitors who stake out spots along the route before dawn each Thanksgiving. Many out-of-town families plan entire trips around the parade. A Saturday march falls on the busiest weekend of the holiday shopping season, which could bring even larger crowds to Midtown as Black Friday weekend shoppers fill the streets around Herald Square.
For the city, the decision also means a second large security operation in one week. Macy's, city officials and law enforcement had held a security briefing on Wednesday for the original Thursday plan, and police will need to redeploy officers, barriers and street closures for Saturday morning.
For Macy's, the timing is especially awkward. The company had spent the year promoting the centennial as a landmark moment for a tradition that has come to signal the start of the holiday shopping season, a role that the parade's Santa Claus finale has symbolized for decades. Holding the event two days later still places it at the heart of that season, and the retailer framed the delay as a chance to celebrate the milestone safely rather than a loss.
The same storm has also prompted high wind warnings in Philadelphia, home to the nation's oldest Thanksgiving parade, and in other cities along the Interstate 95 corridor, where Thanksgiving morning events from parades to Turkey Trot races face the same forecast.
In New York, the immediate task Wednesday night was undoing the day's work. Crews began letting helium out of the balloons that had been laid out under nets along West 77th and West 81st streets, with plans to bring them back to full size on Friday for a parade that, for the first time in 100 years, will be watched by the nation two days after Thanksgiving.

Macy’s made a call on Wednesday, November 25, that it had never made in a century of Thanksgiving mornings. With a nor’easter forecast to hit New York on Thanksgiving Day, the company postponed the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and according to the New York Post and FOX 5 NY, it is the first time in the parade’s history that it has been postponed because of the weather.

The decision came less than two hours after crews had begun filling the balloons with helium, the New York Post reported, and this year’s lineup was built to be special, with a brand-new Snoopy and some balloons from your childhood coming home for the big birthday. Those balloons will have to wait a little longer, and the parade now has a new date.
When Will The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Happen Now?
Macy’s shared the plan in a statement to FOX 5 NY. “With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution,” the company said, “the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28, with an expected step-off at 8:30 a.m.” Macy’s also thanked the “thousands of volunteers, performers and partners” behind the parade, and it said more details will come.

Those numbers matter because the giant balloons live by strict rules. Under the city’s rules, the big balloons can’t fly if sustained winds top 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph, and the NYPD makes the final call on parade morning. Gusts of 30 to 50 mph would blow right past that 34 mph line.
Moving to Saturday gives the 100th parade its chance to go on, balloons and all, once the storm has passed. It also means the families who planned their holiday around it will be watching two days later than usual, on the weekend after the turkey is gone.
Has The Weather Ever Stopped The Parade Before?
The parade has lived through a lot since its first march in 1924, when Macy’s called it the Macy’s Christmas Parade and used it to promote holiday shopping at its flagship store on 34th Street. The only Thanksgivings without it came in 1942, 1943 and 1944, when the parade was suspended during World War II because rubber and helium were needed for the war effort. Wind has beaten the balloons before. In 1971, high winds kept the giant balloons on the ground, the only time the weather has ever grounded them, and the crowds along the route watched a parade without its biggest stars floating overhead.
The windiest memory came in 1997. Strong winds pushed the Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, and falling debris struck a spectator, a woman who spent 24 days in a coma. New York’s leaders answered with new rules on balloon size and wind, and those limits are the reason a few miles per hour can decide so much on Thanksgiving morning.
Then came 2020, when the pandemic turned the parade into a TV-only event. Macy’s closed it to the public and filmed a smaller show around Herald Square, with no crowds lining the sidewalks.
Through the war years, the 1971 winds, the 1997 accident and the strange quiet of 2020, the weather never pushed the parade to a different day. That changed on Wednesday. If you grew up with the parade on in the kitchen while the turkey roasted, Saturday morning will feel a little different this year, with the coffee on and the leftovers in the fridge. Macy's Thanksgiving 2026 Parade Postponed for First Time in 100 Years as Storm Threatens NYC
The parade will move from Thursday to Saturday as forecasts warn of damaging winds, coastal flooding and conditions unsafe for its giant balloons.
A severe coastal storm threatening New York City has prompted Macy's to postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade, disrupting one of America's best-known holiday traditions in what news organisations describe as the event's first weather-related postponement.
The procession will now begin at 8:30 a.m. EST on Saturday, 28 November 2026, instead of Thursday morning. Macy's announced the change on Wednesday after consulting city and agency partners, saying: 'The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority.' The decision came as crews were inflating the parade's giant balloons on Manhattan's Upper West Side.
Dangerous Winds Force a Historic Decision
The National Weather Service (NWS) has placed Manhattan and the rest of New York City under a High Wind Warning from 10 a.m. on Thursday until 1 a.m. on Friday. Its Wednesday afternoon bulletin forecast easterly winds of 25–35mph, with gusts of up to 60mph. 'Damaging winds will blow down trees and power lines,' the agency warned.
Forecasters also expect widespread moderate coastal flooding around Thursday's high tides. The agency's Wednesday morning discussion placed the strongest winds in the afternoon and evening, although it noted some uncertainty over timing. City emergency officials had warned on Tuesday that one to two inches (25–51mm) of rain could fall.
Concern had been building before the announcement. 'This is a challenging week. This is a challenging forecast,' New York City Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell told WABC, while raising an earlier start as one option. As the forecast cast doubt over the balloons, NWS meteorologist Joe Pollina told Gothamist: 'They should be concerned.'
A Centennial Celebration Is Put on Hold
The parade made its debut in 1924, and was suspended from 1942 to 1944 during the Second World War. This year therefore marks the 100th edition, although 102 years have passed since the first. Weather grounded the giant character balloons in 1971, but PIX11 reports that the parade has never previously moved to a different day.
The disruption strikes an edition designed to feature a record 100 inflatables and more than 11,000 volunteers and participants. Sharon Otterman, Macy's chief marketing officer, had promised 'a celebration of unprecedented scale' in a 13 November announcement. The planned attractions include Bluey, Sorcerer's Apprentice Mickey and Underdog along a 2.5-mile (4km) route.
For one spectator attending Wednesday's balloon inflation, the postponement was particularly disappointing. 'It's super disappointing, especially since it's the 100th anniversary,' the onlooker told ABC7. The march had been due to travel from the Upper West Side to Macy's Herald Square flagship, where Megan Moroney and Teddy Swims were scheduled to perform.
Balloon Safety Rules Rooted in a 1997 Accident
Wind poses a particular danger to the parade's towering balloons. Under safety measures introduced in 1998, large balloons are prohibited from flying when sustained winds exceed 23mph or gusts exceed 34mph, and police have the final say on public safety. Thursday's forecast exceeds both thresholds, although the NWS warning does not begin until 90 minutes after the original start time.
City officials adopted those measures after the 1997 parade, when high winds propelled a Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost on Central Park West. Then-Mayor Rudolph Giuliani said a task force had examined the parade to ensure that 'the tragic accident which occurred last year does not happen again'. The lawsuit that followed the accident alleged that the collision dislodged part of the post, which struck spectators including Kathleen Caronna, who suffered serious head injuries.
A later court ruling recounted testimony that a Macy's parade official had assured Police Chief James Tuller that company employees could handle the balloons in the prevailing winds. Tuller subsequently decided that the parade could safely proceed. On 13 February 2001, New York State Supreme Court Justice Joan Madden dismissed parade-related negligence claims against the city on governmental immunity grounds, although a claim concerning lamppost maintenance was allowed to continue. Caronna later settled her lawsuit on the eve of jury selection, according to her lawyer.
Saturday Plans and Holiday Disruption
Macy's said its team was still working through the logistics and would share further details once they were finalised. NBC will air a repeat of the 2025 parade on Thanksgiving Day, with this year's procession rescheduled for Saturday. Anyone planning to attend in person on Saturday should check official updates on timings and arrangements before travelling.
Wednesday morning's NWS aviation outlook showed westerly winds at area airports gusting to about 23–29mph on Saturday. That range sits below the 34 mph gust threshold for grounding balloons, but it does not guarantee conditions along the parade route. Officials will also need to consider sustained wind speeds.
The storm's consequences extend well beyond the parade, with city emergency officials warning of flooded coastal roads, falling branches and possible flight delays. '[W]e want every New Yorker to get there and back safely,' Mayor Zohran Mamdani said of holiday travel in a Tuesday advisory issued before the postponement.
After a century of marches, New York's milestone celebration must now wait two more days.

Macy's 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed due to weather forecast
NEW YORK (TNND) — Macy's postponed its Thanksgiving Day Parade by a few days due to an approaching nor'easter.
It marked the first weather-related postponement in the event's history. The parade balloons were grounded only once due to weather in 1971.
The 100th annual parade was scheduled for Thursday in New York City, but organizers shifted the event to Saturday morning instead.
"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," a Macy’s spokesperson said in a statement, per The New york Post.
"Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year," the statement noted. "We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday."
In a news conference on Wednesday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the city is expecting heavy rain and severe wind on Thursday, urging New Yorkers to use caution while traveling that day. Mamdani said that he knew people would be disappointed that the parade was postponed, but that holding the event on Saturday, with better weather conditions, would be fun and safe.
Earlier this week, Macy’s said it was monitoring the forecast with city and agency partners. The company reportedly said decisions about whether the parade's giant balloons could fly would be made based on weather conditions and safety protocols.
The New York Post reported crews had filled the balloons with helium less than two hours before the decision to delay the parade, as strong winds can make the balloons difficult to control. New York City safety rules require them to be grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph.
The storm was expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to the New York area on Thanksgiving.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed due to weather for first time ever
NEW YORK - The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to the nor'easter, marking the first time the parade was moved because of weather.
Thanksgiving parade postponed
Big picture view:
Macy's has confirmed that the parade will be postponed to this Saturday, Nov. 28, at 8:30 a.m.
The NYPD held the final say on whether the balloons could fly. Under New York City safety guidelines, large parade balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts surpass 34 mph.
What they're saying:
Macy's provided a statement regarding the decision to FOX 5 NY:
"With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed.
In close coordination with our City and agency partners, the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28, with an expected step-off at 8:30 a.m.
Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized.
We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday."
FOX 5 NY's Richard Giacovas spoke to spectators who were excited to see the parade tomorrow – children expressed their disappointment at the fact that the parade has been postponed.
Giacovas is also reporting that the balloons will be deflated tonight, and will then be reinflated at some point this Friday, Nov. 27.
Thanksgiving weather in NYC
Local perspective:
According to the National Weather Service and the FOX Forecast Center, a low-pressure system moving northward along the Eastern Seaboard is likely bringing 1 to 2 inches of rain to the Tri-State area from Thursday into early Friday.
Key impacts for New York, New Jersey and Connecticut include:
- Damaging winds: Wind gusts are forecast to reach 30 to 50 mph across the region – prompting a High Wind Watch for Manhattan – and up to 60 mph along the Jersey Shore.
- Heavy rain and flooding: Rapidly deteriorating conditions on Thursday are raising concerns about flash flooding and moderate-to-widespread coastal flooding before the storm clears out early Friday morning.
- Timing: Forecasters noted that while the heaviest rain and strongest winds could hold off until the second half of Thanksgiving Day, unsafe wind conditions along the parade route forced the balloons to be grounded.
(Photo: Getty Images)
The Source: This story was written with information from the NYPD, Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade organizers, FOX Weather, the National Weather Service and historical parade records.

sources.news_title: Macy’s parade moved to Saturday due to weather conditions
sources.text:
NEW YORK — Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: Organizers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday because of bad weather.
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved "out of an abundance of caution" and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy's said in a statement Wednesday.
"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the company said.
The postponement came as New York City is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade's massive balloons would fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
Safety comes first, says Mayor Mamdani
At a news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday's winds will be strong enough to snap tree limbs and down power lines, and he stressed that rescheduling the parade was the right call.
"Now, I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," he said. "Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first."
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday. The city's emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty tractor-trailers from bridges Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event's expansive lineup would also shift to the new date, though representatives for Broadway shows "Chicago" and "Hamilton" said their performers will make the switch to Saturday.
The parade's iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy's representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city's news media ahead of the official postponement.
Will Coss, a Macy's executive, said organizers are working with bands and other performers and are "optimistic that we're going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce and to deliver to New York City on Thanksgiving."
"Everyone understands what we're up against and is rallying behind us to create the best and most successful 100th parade," he said.
Parade's delay is a silver lining for one youngster
While the delay may have scrambled some parade-goers' plans, the clouds had a silver lining for at least one youngster.
Sarah Collins and her youngest son have been looking forward to a New York weekend trip to celebrate his recent 12th birthday. But since their flight from Florida arrives Friday, the parade wasn't part of their original plans. Now, it is, and he's excited.
"It's been his lifelong wish to go to New York and see all the Christmas stuff," she said in a message.
A spokesperson for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was canceled for three years — in 1942, 1943 and 1944 — during World War II, the spokesperson said.
The parade balloons have been grounded only once due to weather, in 1971.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma. Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy's said in a statement.

I was a clown in the Thanksgiving Day Parade — here’s what you don’t see

I am standing in the middle of Manhattan with my face covered in clown makeup, holding a gigantic bright red ribbon. I’ve never been colder in my life. Next to me is the famous weatherman Al Roker, a Macy’s executive and … a robot. I spend the next hour running through the city streets pouring confetti on strangers before crossing Herald Square with an exhale: I’ve just completed my second Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
Participating in one of the most iconic events in American history isn’t for the faint of heart; there’s training to attend, campy makeup to apply and, for some of us, childhood circus trauma to overcome. But being a clown, I can also confirm, it’s a lot of fun.
One of the most thrilling aspects of the parade, though, is what doesn’t get seen on television — like the preparation for the big day. For my first year in the parade in 2012, I attended Clown University to master the hijinks of clowning around alongside about a dozen of my family members, all participating in the parade as a reunion of sorts.
As part of the “Funny Bones Medical Team” clown group — the parade clowns all have designated groups with themed costumes — we learned a dance routine to the Bee Gees track “Stayin’ Alive,” which we performed periodically along the parade route. The professional clowns gave us tips on everything from how to preserve your limited confetti supply to – more crucially – how not to scare small children.
Then, a few weeks later, it’s showtime.
For us clowns, the parade day starts long before the sun rises. Traveling from Long Island meant a very early train to make the 5 a.m. call time. We shuffled in and out of a Midtown Manhattan hotel, exchanging street clothes and fresh faces for costumes and clown makeup. We submitted measurements ahead of time to help the wardrobe teams do some advanced planning. But the morning of, it’s a fast and furious dash to be matched with a costume from the hundreds of garments hanging on hundreds of clothing racks. None of this is shown during the broadcast, but it’s a spectacle of its own, since more than 11,000 volunteers are involved each year.
Then we wait. Performers are placed at designated meeting points in and around Central Park, primed to join the parade route. It’s a great time to snap photos (and practice that dance routine) — none of which you’ll see on the broadcast, but trust that it’s happening.
It was especially meaningful to participate in the 2012 parade as it was held only weeks after Hurricane Sandy devastated the region. I’ll never forget that a special spectator section for those affected by the storm was set up that year at 59th Street, where we were urged to sprinkle a bit more confetti on those who had lost so much. It was so moving to see their reactions and to have a hand in helping them forget about their troubles, even if for a fleeting moment.
The parade that year was a glorious (and definitely too hot in a clown costume) 70F, which would prove to be a stark contrast for my return the next year. The 2013 parade remains the coldest I’ve ever been in my life, at 29F with a wind chill index of around 13F.
Frostbite be damned, I was a Celebration Clown and had the privilege of holding the ribbon during the parade’s opening ceremony, standing next to Roker as the robot cut the ribbon.
It was much the same as the previous year — with the too-early call time to get clown-ified before being ushered to the parade route — just much, much colder. Even wearing layers under my clown costume wasn’t enough of a shield from the bitter chill that engulfed my body for hours afterward.
After finishing the 2.5-mile jaunt along the parade route, it’s a mad dash to get out of costume and race back to the Long Island Rail Road in time for dinner. By then, I’d been up for about eight or nine hours, had barely eaten, and was pretty dehydrated after running thousands of steps through Manhattan.
Recovery looked like a hot shower at home and wearing a warm sweater to stuff myself silly at Thanksgiving dinner while recounting the day to my family.
But at the dinner table that night — after both years in the parade — I had more to be thankful for after my time clowning around.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” parade sponsor Macy’s wrote in a statement.
“Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, November 28.”
Millions of people typically gather to catch a glimpse of the festivities
Each year, the parade’s towering balloons and performances trace a roughly 4km route from Midtown Manhattan to Macy’s Herald Square flagship store on 34th Street.
Millions of people typically gather to catch a glimpse of the festivities.
It is the first time in its history that it has been postponed, The New York Post reported.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned that the system could bring dangerous conditions across the city as he addressed a safety briefing.
“This will be a heavy storm. We are expecting sustained winds between 30 and 40 miles per hour, with gusts as high as 60 to 65 miles per hour possible,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a safety briefing.
“The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning as well as a coastal flood warning.
“Winds will be strong enough to down tree limbs and power lines.”
Organisers would have been only too aware of what high winds can do, after gusts battered the parade in 1997.
That year, volunteers struggled but failed to keep a tight rein on ropes which constantly threatened to slam into onlookers.
The careening 18-foot figure of the “Cat in the Hat” – from the popular children’s book – toppled a lamppost, knocking one bystander unconscious.
Another balloon, the purple dinosaur known to children as “Barney,” went out of control prompting police armed with scissors to puncture and deflate the balloon.
New York City police rush to the aid of the Pink Panther balloon as it collapses to high winds in 1997
Yet another casualty was the “Pink Panther” balloon, which blew up over 42nd Street, sending shreds of pink rubber confetti raining on bystanders.
Macy’s parade executive producer Will Coss said the decision, while difficult, was driven by safety concerns for everyone involved.

NEW YORK (AP) — Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade will also be a first: Organizers made an unprecedented decision to postpone the event to Saturday because of bad weather.
The annual parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, has been moved “out of an abundance of caution” and following consultation with city officials about the severe weather, Macy’s said in a statement Wednesday.
“Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized,” the company said.
The postponement came as New York City is set to get slammed by a storm bringing intense winds and rain to the region, which had raised worries about how the parade’s massive balloonswould fare while floating through the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers and over throngs of spectators lining the streets below.
Safety comes first, says Mayor Mamdani
At a news conference, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday’s winds will be strong enough to snap tree limbs and down power lines, and he stressed that rescheduling the parade was the right call.
“Now, I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow,” he said. “Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first.”
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday. The city’s emergency management agency has been warning residents about the possible storm, with officials banning empty tractor-trailers from bridges Thursday morning because of the wind.
NBC, which airs the parade, said it will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether the event’s expansive lineup would also shift to the new date, though representatives for Broadway shows “Chicago” and “Hamilton” said their performers will make the switch to Saturday.
The parade’s iconic balloons were well on the way to being inflated when the postponement was announced. Macy’s representatives had repeatedly put off interviews on-site, raising eyebrows among the city’s news media ahead of the official postponement.
Will Coss, a Macy’s executive, said organizers are working with bands and other performers and are “optimistic that we’re going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce and to deliver to New York City on Thanksgiving.”
“Everyone understands what we’re up against and is rallying behind us to create the best and most successful 100th parade,” he said.
Parade’s delay is a silver lining for one youngster
While the delay may have scrambled some parade-goers’ plans, the clouds had a silver lining for at least one youngster.
Sarah Collins and her youngest son have been looking forward to a New York weekend trip to celebrate his recent 12th birthday. But since their flight from Florida arrives Friday, the parade wasn’t part of their original plans. Now, it is, and he’s excited.
“It’s been his lifelong wish to go to New York and see all the Christmas stuff,” she said in a message.
A spokesperson for the retail giant said it was the first time the event has been postponed. It was canceled for three years — in 1942, 1943 and 1944 — during World War II, the spokesperson said.
The parade balloons have been grounded only once due to weather, in 1971.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower the balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The rules were put in place after high winds sent a balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma. Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.
The rescheduled parade will kick off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday, Macy’s said in a statement.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani struck a personal note during a press briefing Wednesday about the postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade due to a major storm.
“Many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow,” the mayor said. “I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first. On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker, and everyone visiting, will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”
Organizers and city officials, made the call earlier Wednesday to push the 100th annual edition of the parade to Saturday morning, when the forecast calls for sunny skies and temperatures in the 40s. A Nor’easter, a classic storm pattern, is expected to bring drenching rain and high winds to New York and many other parts of the Northeast on Thursday and into Friday. Forecasters are calling for as much as 2 inches of rain in New York, which would make it among the wettest Thanksgivings ever in the city.
Officials have rules in place preventing balloons from proceeding down city streets when sustained winds are 25 mph or higher, or if gusts top 35 mph.
Watch on Deadline
Mamdani, hobbled by a recent Achilles tear, said he will miss Saturday’s parade due to pending surgery and “doctor’s orders.” But while he walked with a limp, the mayor showed he hadn’t lost a step mentally. When a reporter asked about the blowing up of the signature balloons, an annual public ritual held on Thanksgiving Eve near the parade route, Mamdani quipped, “It’s the only kind of inflation we support in New York City.”
Will Coss, an executive producer and VP at Macy’s who oversees the retailer’s events, said there will not be a second chance to watch the night-before inflation of the balloons due to the complex logistics of the postponement. He was also asked about the lineup for the event, which could change given that some marching bands (like the one from the University of Albama) are planning to leave town to play at college football games or other events.
The parade is set to include a number of other special guests and celebrities appearing on floats or performing. An “All-Star Broadway Thanksgiving Day Celebration” will feature performers from new and long-running Broadway productions in a special 10-minute medley.
Coss said it is “an evolving conversation” about potential replacements or planned participants possibly bowing out due to conflicts or travel plans. “We’ve been in communication with all of our participants, from our bands, to our performance groups, to our performing talent. We are optimistic that we’re going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce, and to deliver to New York City.”
The parade remains a major TV draw, with last year’s pulling in 34.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, its biggest combined audience on record. By slotting it in on Saturday morning from 8:30 a.m. to noon ET, NBC should be able to have access to a good-sized audience before college football takes over. Still, the viewership patterns on a more conventional Saturday morning versus those on a weekday holiday with preparations for the Thanksgiving feast providing a supply of captive viewers, will be interesting to watch.
In place of the live event, NBC and Peacock will re-air the 2025 edition of the parade on Thursday morning. Mindful of the unusual dynamic in play this year, the network and streamer will double-run the same ads on both Thursday and Saturday to ensure the scale and impact nets out to a satisfying level for buyers.
It is the first time since it began in 1924 that the parade has ever been postponed. In 1971, balloons were grounded by inclement weather but the parade was still held. World War II forced the cancellation of the parade from 1942 to 1944, and the Covid pandemic in 2020 led to organizers converting it into a television-only event around the Herald Square location of Macy’s Department Store.
This year’s parade is especially significant to Macy’s and NBC, with the latter celebrating its centennial in broadcasting. To help mark the milestone, the parade is set to have 100 of its trademark large balloons.
The importance of NBC’s 100th anniversary is likely to have played a role in the rescheduling. Parent company NBCUniversal, announced early this week that this year’s parade set a revenue record. A windswept and soggy edition of the annual TV fixture would surely have presented myriad production challenges. It possibly would also have left advertisers tuning in to see compromised signage and balloons (some of them branded) swirling precariously around the streets.
“We want to ensure that we’re delivering a parade that’s not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn’t come at the expense of anyone’s safety,” Mamdani said.

It’s a historic call. The parade has never before been postponed because of weather.
Why was the Macy’s parade postponed?
Wind, mostly, plus a lot of rain. New York City emergency management officials expect wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph on Thursday, with sustained winds of 30 to 38 mph and moderate to heavy rain, The Associated Press reported. The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning running from Thursday into Friday.
Those conditions are a nightmare for giant helium balloons. The city has rules to lower balloons or cancel their flights when winds get too strong, because gusts can shove them off course and into crowds. Those rules came after serious balloon accidents in 1997 and 2005.
In its statement, NBC said the city, Macy’s and NBC made the decision “in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators.” A Macy’s spokesperson said the team is working through the logistics and will share details as they’re finalized.
Weren’t the balloons already inflated?
Yes, and that’s part of what makes this so wild. The decision came less than two hours after crews filled the balloons with helium on the Upper West Side for their morning flight, according to sources cited in a report carried by Yahoo News.
Balloon inflation on West 77th and West 81st streets is a beloved Thanksgiving Eve tradition that draws thousands of spectators. Fans who showed up Wednesday still got to see the giants come to life. They’ll just have to wait until Saturday to see them fly.
Has the Macy’s parade ever been canceled before?
Only during World War II. The parade was suspended from 1942 to 1944, CBS New York noted. Beyond that, it has marched every Thanksgiving since it began in 1924 as the Macy’s Christmas Parade.
Weather has caused trouble before, though. Balloons were grounded once, in 1971, when high winds kept them from flying. Earlier this week, as the storm forecast came into focus, there was serious talk that the balloons might be grounded again this year. Postponing the whole parade lets Macy’s keep its centennial show intact.
What will NBC air on Thanksgiving morning?
NBC will rerun last year’s 99th parade on Thursday, the network said. That broadcast was hosted by Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker, and it set a viewership record with 34.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, according to TheWrap.

Whether every performer can make the new date is still an open question. Marching bands and performers who planned around Thursday now have to rework their travel, and Macy’s hasn’t released an updated lineup.
What should spectators do now?
Hold off on that early alarm Thursday. The parade won’t run Thanksgiving morning, and the storm is the bigger concern for anyone heading outdoors.
If you’re in New York for the holiday and can stay through the weekend, the parade route will be the place to be Saturday morning. Crowds usually start lining up hours before the 8:30 a.m. start, and Saturday could be even busier since many people are off work.
Keep an eye on Macy’s and NBC for any changes to the route, start time or performer lineup.

Volunteers had just finished inflating the balloons near the American Museum of Natural History on Wednesday afternoon when the official word came down. Macy’s said the safety of participants and spectators is its top priority and that the decision followed close consultation with city and agency partners. The parade is now expected to step off at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday along its usual 2.5 mile route from West 77th Street and Central Park West down to Herald Square.
What Airs on Thanksgiving Morning Instead

Macy’s says its team is still working through the operational logistics of the move and will share final details as they are set.
New York is not the only city adjusting. Philadelphia’s Thanksgiving Day Parade organizers also decided against flying their balloons this year out of an abundance of caution as the same storm system moves up the East Coast.
Disney Was Set to Have a Big Year in the Parade
Disney fans had plenty to watch for in the 100th parade, and the good news is it is all still happening, just two days later. Disney Cruise Line is debuting a brand new float this year, topped with a Sorcerer Mickey inspired funnel and characters from Mickey Mouse and friends to Jessie from Toy Story and Mirabel from Encanto. The Sorcerer Mickey balloon is also part of this year’s balloon lineup, and crowd favorites like the Buzz Lightyear balloon, pictured above over Times Square, remain parade staples.
Disney’s history in the parade stretches back decades, as the vintage shot of the Donald Duck and Mickey Mouse balloons shows. If you are looking for Disney’s own parade fix on a holiday, the Wonderful World of Disney Holiday Spectacular airs Monday night on ABC, and you can check the full parade details on the official Macy’s parade page as Saturday plans are finalized.
I will be honest, Thanksgiving morning without the live parade feels a little off, it is the background of the whole day in our house. But 60 mph gusts and five story tall balloons do not mix, and Saturday morning with the whole family still in town might end up being a pretty great rain date. See you at 8:30 on Saturday.

sources.text:
Did you know it took Bugs Bunny 49 years from his debut to get a balloon in the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade? That was far too long for the world’s most beloved rabbit, but there are so many popular characters like Bugs who never had a balloon.
These are the top picks for characters that would make amazing balloons in the country’s biggest parade.
- TWEETY BIRD
  Woodstock was not the only popular yellow bird in fiction. Tweety Bird, the lovable cartoon icon, deserves his moment to fly high this Thanksgiving. Despite his enormous size as a balloon, Sylvester the Cat would probably still try to put him on the menu instead of turkey.
- TOM AND JERRY
  While Tweety Bird would fly solo, this inseparable cartoon duo would debut together. Tom Cat and Jerry Mouse still have relevance today as classic cartoon characters. Imagine the chaos that would ensue if these two wove through skyscrapers.
- TINKER BELL
  Every Thanksgiving needs faith, trust and pixie dust. Since her 1953 debut in “Peter Pan,” Tinker Bell has become a strong character for girls to look up to. The world felt magical when I watched her movies as a child, and her parade balloon could bring that feeling to everyone who watched.
- THE POWERPUFF GIRLS
  With sugar, spice and everything nice and awesome superpowers, these cartoon sisters also inspired many girls. Blossom, Buttercup and Bubbles would fit right into the urban New York atmosphere. Instead of facing Mojo Jojo, they might have to look out for King Kong instead.
- TAILS
  Sonic took part in the parade multiple times, but now his sidekick should get a turn. Tails, the brains behind the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, would be a great addition to the parade. Whether in a plane or flying with his two fuzzy tails, this adorable character would fit right in.
- KIRBY
  The parade needs more adorable video game characters. With his round shape, Kirby would be the perfect candidate for a balloon. The parade planners should proceed with caution to ensure he does not try to swallow the parade-goers.
- BAYMAX
  Another lovable character that would make a great balloon would be everybody’s favorite personal healthcare companion. Baymax, a modern character compared to the rest of this list, quickly became a cartoon icon. His presence in the parade would ensure that nobody got too bloated from their Thanksgiving meal.
- APPA
  “Avatar: The Last Airbender” created numerous fictional species, from winged lemurs to turtle ducks. Appa, the main cast’s loyal flying bison, would be an amazing spectacle in the parade. Everyone could say “Appa, yip yip!” as he soars through the city skies.
- GENIE FROM “ALADDIN”
  The Macy’s parade always does a great job with music. From marching bands to Broadway performances, many people watch to hear the show tunes over the balloons. Genie would be a perfect connector between the two and could feature a great musical performance like “Friend Like Me.”
- SAILOR MOON
  This magical girl would bring more sparkle to everybody’s Thanksgiving celebrations. Some consider Sailor Moon a key anime that popularized the genre in the United States. One anime, “Dragon Ball,” made its way to the parade, so Sailor Moon would be a great addition to celebrate this genre. 
While there are many more characters that deserve a balloon, these are the ones that deserve the spotlight the most.
Whether because they have gone too long without recognition or because they would be a sight to behold, these characters would make the future Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade even better.

sources.news_title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed To Saturday Due To Expected Bad Weather
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Saturday as powerful winds are expected to bear down on New York during the annual event, NBC said Wednesday.
In a statement, NBC said the parade would now be held on Saturday, citing conversations with the city and concerns over the safety of participants and spectators.
“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided, in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday,” the statement said.
NBC, which airs the parade, will instead broadcast a rerun of the 2025 edition Thursday.
New York City is expected to get blasted with wind gusts between 50 to 60 mph (80 to 96 kph) on Thursday, along with steady, sustained winds between 30 to 38 mph (48 to 61 kph), according to city emergency management officials. Moderate to heavy rain is also expected.
Separately, the National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for Thursday into Friday.
The city has long had measures in place that dictate whether to lower balloons or cancel their flights entirely if the wind gets too strong, due to concerns that strong winds can knock them off course and into spectators along the parade route.
The city’s balloon rules were put in place after high winds sent a Cat in the Hat balloon careening into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma.
The parade was scheduled to kick off at 8:30 a.m. Macy’s had said a decision on whether to fly the balloons would be made on the morning of the parade.
City rules have long barred large balloons from flying if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or gusts exceed 34 mph (55 kph).
The measures were implemented after a balloon careened into a lamppost near Central Park and critically injured a woman in 1997. The parade has seen other snafus since then, including a 2005 incident in which a balloon hit a lamppost and hurt a woman and her young sister.
Bad weather in the past has caused balloons to be flown a bit lower than usual, with each inflatable character having a distinct risk profile that includes its size and weight and optimal altitudes for differing wind speeds.

sources.text:
If your Thanksgiving morning plans include the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, you’ll have to wait a couple of extra days.
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday, Nov. 28, because of severe weather expected in New York City on Thanksgiving Day. The parade is now expected to step off at 8:30 a.m. Saturday.
“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said in a statement Wednesday, Nov. 25. “Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28. We expect the Parade to kick off at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.”
It’s the first time the parade has been moved to a different day since it began in 1924.
What’s on TV Thursday morning
You’ll still see a parade on TV Thanksgiving morning, just not this year’s.
NBC said it will air the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Thursday at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones. In a statement, the network said the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC made the decision together “in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators.” NBC said more details will follow.
Broadcast details for Saturday’s parade had not been announced as of Wednesday afternoon. The parade normally airs on NBC and streams on Peacock, with Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker hosting.
A big year for a big storm
The timing is especially tough for the parade’s centennial. Macy’s planned a record 100 balloons and inflatables for the 100th edition.
The parade has faced bad weather before. In 1971, wind and rain kept the giant balloons grounded, but the parade itself went on. It was also suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II, when the rubber and helium used for the balloons were needed for the war effort. But until now, the parade had never been moved off Thanksgiving Day.
Storm hitting Alexandria, too
The same coastal storm is expected to bring a soggy, blustery Thanksgiving to the D.C. area. The National Weather Service is forecasting rain on Thanksgiving Day, with a high near 60 and northeast winds of 22 to 26 mph with gusts as high as 47 mph.

2026 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Delayed to Saturday
The parade has been postponed due to weather.
November 25, 2026 By Margaret Hall
The 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been delayed due to inclement weather. Rather than being held on Thanksgiving, November 26, the parade will now be held Saturday, November 28.
Per Macy's, "Our team is working through the operational logistics for this change and will share details as they are finalized. The parade is expected to begin at 8:30 A.M. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday." Playbill will share more information as it becomes available.
On November 26, NBC will re-air the 2025 Thanksgiving Day parade at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.
Though the parade has been pushed forward to Saturday, Broadway favorite Amber Iman will still be taking over Playbill's Instagram throughout the parade for live commentary, colorful observations, and play-by-play analysis of the Parade—all from the comfort of her couch.
The parade was set to include a 10-minute medley of theatre performances taking viewers "on a musical journey through Broadway past and present, filled with beloved songs and Easter eggs for theatre fans to discover along the way," per press notes.
For the Broadway number, performers were expected from The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and Wicked. The musical Rent, celebrating its 30th anniversary, was also set be part of the medley (and the only musical not currently running on Broadway). Press notes also listed Paddington the Musical amongst expected parade float appearances, separate from the Broadway medley.
It is not clear at this time if performers will still be able to participate in the rescheduled parade, given the typical two-show-day schedule on Saturdays for most Broadway shows. Playbill will update this article as we receive more information.
If you want to see a show this weekend, check out Playbill's Thanksgiving Week Broadway show schedule. Have a very happy Thanksgiving.

sources.news_title: Updated: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed Until Saturday Due to Incoming Storm; What to Know
sources.text:
Update: Wednesday, 5:45 p.m. — “New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy’s have decided to postpone the annual Thanksgiving Day parade,” according to ABC News and multiple other sources. “The parade will now step off on Saturday, November 28th, at 8:30 a.m.,” ABC reported.
The reason for the change is “a powerful coastal storm that will impact the Tri-State Area on Thanksgiving,” wrote CBS News. “Rain is expected to develop in the morning, just as the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade would have gotten underway. Wind gusts of 30 to 45 mph will accompany the rain through the morning hours.”
This is the first time in its 100-year history that the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed.
“In the past, balloons have been grounded due to high winds, but the parade has never previously been postponed due to weather,” CBS noted. “A city official said the balloons [that have already been inflated] will be deflated starting at 7 p.m. [tonight] and will be re-inflated on Friday afternoon.”
More details are expected during a 6 p.m. news conference with the mayor, police commissioner, and Macy’s executives.
By Gus Saltonstall
The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is slated to set off Thursday morning for its 100th rendition of the event.
The parade will begin at 8:30 a.m. from the Upper West Side at West 76th Street and Central Park West and proceed to journey two-and-a-half miles downtown to Macy’s flagship Herald Square store on West 34th Street.
For those who are looking to attend the parade in person, you can find the best places to watch the parade — HERE.
The parade is also broadcast live Thursday morning on NBC or Peacock.
But what about the weather?
The Thanksgiving Day Parade will take place rain or shine, but whether or not the balloons wil fly remains up in the air.
A storm is set to hit the city beginning around 6 a.m. on Thursday, bringing with it sustained high winds of over 40 miles per hour and gusts of over 60 miles per hour. If there are sustained winds of over 34 miles per hour, the balloons will be grounded.
It would be the first time since 1971 that Macy’s was forced to ground the balloons due to bad weather.
Organizers have told multiple publications, including the New York Post, that they will not decide on whether the balloons will fly in the parade until Thursday morning. That means the balloon inflation event on Wednesday will still take place.
